## Hepatocellular Carcinoma
- Most common primary liver tumor
- Approximately 800,000 deaths globally per year
- Fourth leading cause of cancer death worldwide
- Sixth most common neoplasia
- Marked geographic differences in incidence

## Chapter Overview
- Epidemiology, risk factors, and prevention
- Molecular profile
- Screening strategies
- Clinical presentation
- Diagnosis
- Staging and prognostic evaluation
- Treatment approaches
- Future prospects

## Global Burden
- Liver tumors are a major global health problem
- Incidence exceeds 20 cases per 100,000 population in high-risk areas
- High-risk areas include Asia and sub-Saharan Africa
- Incidence and mortality are increasing in many regions
- Decreasing incidence reported in Japan

## Geographic Variation
- Asia and sub-Saharan Africa: high-risk areas
- North America, Latin America, and Central Europe: increasing rates
- Japan: decreasing rates
- Geographic distribution linked to hepatitis viruses and environmental pathogens
- Majority of cases occur in sub-Saharan Africa and West Asia

## Sex and Age Distribution
- Prevalence is 3-fold higher in males than females
- Peak incidence around sixth and seventh decade of life
- Incidence varies by region and ethnicity
- Risk factors differ across populations
- Sex differences may reflect exposure and hormonal factors

## Underlying Chronic Liver Disease
- HCC usually develops in the setting of chronic liver disease
- Cirrhosis is the major determinant
- Main background etiologies:
  - Chronic hepatitis B
  - Chronic hepatitis C
  - Alcoholic liver disease
  - Metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease
- Other causes include alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and hereditary hemochromatosis

## Changing Etiology
- Universal HBV vaccination is reshaping risk
- Direct-acting antivirals against HCV are widely used
- MAFLD-associated comorbidities are increasing
- Obesity, diabetes, and dyslipidemia frequently overlap with alcohol consumption
- Risk factor burden is changing globally

## Survival Rates
- 5-year survival rate is between 5% and 15%
- Reflects challenging management
- Many patients diagnosed at advanced stage
- Curative options limited to early stages
- Recurrence remains a major concern

## Epidemiology: Cirrhosis as Major Determinant
- Cirrhosis is the major determinant of HCC
- Causes include viral infections, MAFLD, alcohol, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and hereditary hemochromatosis
- One-third of cirrhosis patients will develop HCC in their lifetime
- Annual risk is 1% to 8% depending on etiology
- Risk is greater with more severe liver disease

## Annual HCC Risk in Cirrhosis
- Annual risk ranges from 1% to 8%
- Depends on underlying etiology
- Higher risk with more relevant signs of liver disease
- Higher risk with more severe liver disease
- All cirrhosis patients are at risk

## Geographic Distribution and Aflatoxin
- Majority of cases occur in sub-Saharan Africa and West Asia
- High prevalence of HBV infection
- Exposure to aflatoxin B1
- Aflatoxin is a mycotoxin produced by Aspergillus species
- Induces a specific p53 mutation that offers proliferation advantages

## HBV-Related Risk Factors
- High viral load
- Active viral replication
- Genotype C
- Presence of liver dysfunction
- HBV-related HCC can develop without cirrhosis in 20% to 30% of cases
- Inactive HBV carriers are also at increased risk
- HBV gene integration into host genome contributes to risk

## HBV Vaccination Impact
- Significant impact on reducing HCC-related deaths
- Reported in endemic areas such as Taiwan
- Universal HBV vaccination is a key preventive strategy
- Reduces HBV-related HCC burden
- Remains a major public health success

## HCV as Risk Factor
- Main risk factor in Japan and Western countries
- Especially Europe and United States
- HCC in HCV occurs almost exclusively with advanced liver disease or cirrhosis
- HCV treatment decreases but does not eliminate HCC risk
- Sustained virologic response is associated with reduced HCC risk

## HCV Treatment and HCC Risk
- Direct-acting antivirals induce sustained virologic response at higher rates than interferon-based regimens
- Meta-analysis shows sustained virologic response reduces HCC risk
- HCV-related HCC rate expected to decrease or stabilize
- Patients with sustained virologic response after HCV treatment must remain under screening
- Risk is not eliminated

## DAA Controversy
- Hypothesis: DAAs in patients previously treated for HCC may be related to early recurrences
- Aggressive biological behavior has been suggested
- Raises concern about wide applicability of DAAs in patients with past HCC
- Highly controversial issue
- Major heterogeneity between studies prevents robust conclusion

## MAFLD as Emerging Risk Factor
- Growing evidence that MAFLD is increasingly frequent in HCC patients
- Often associated with obesity, hypertension, and diabetes
- Clearly overlaps with alcohol consumption
- Likely causes HCC via cirrhosis
- Precise pathogenesis not fully elucidated
- Some cases occur in absence of cirrhosis

## US Transplant Registry Trends
- National United States registry on liver transplantations 2002–2016
- HCV and alcohol etiologies remained stable
- HBV decreased
- Relevant increase in non-alcoholic steatohepatitis
- Now grouped under MAFLD
- Projects ascending burden of MAFLD-related HCC

## MAFLD and Cardiovascular Mortality
- Main cause of death in MAFLD patients is cardiovascular events
- Stresses need for multiorgan approach
- Beyond individual specialties
- Manage metabolic syndrome and liver disease together
- Preventive strategies must address cardiovascular risk

## Protective Factors
- HBV vaccination
- Antiviral treatment for HBV and HCV
- Proper controls in healthcare settings prevent HCV dissemination
- Alcohol intake should be targeted by health campaigns
- Aflatoxin contamination prevented by avoiding grain storage in humid conditions
- Obesity epidemic must be controlled by health education

## Prevention: Primary
- HBV vaccination
- Educational programs
- Anti-alcohol campaigns
- Control of diabetes, obesity, and dyslipidemia
- Testing high-risk groups for viral hepatitis
- Reduce aflatoxin exposure

## Prevention: Secondary
- Prior recognition of affected individuals
- No proof of cost-effectiveness of population screening for liver disease
- Semiannual screening for at-risk patients
- Antiviral therapy
- Stop alcohol
- Control metabolic risk factors

## Chemoprevention Signals
- Observational studies support statins reduce HCC risk
- Aspirin may reduce HCC risk
- Coffee consumption may reduce HCC risk
- Additional evidence needed
- Unclear if alimentary or pharmacologic measures reduce HCC risk

## Molecular Profile: Overview
- Hepatocarcinogenesis is complex
- Several molecular landmarks and signaling pathways involved
- Genomic analyses predominantly restricted to early-stage resected HCC
- May not reflect intermediate and advanced stages
- Accumulating knowledge of initiation and progression

## Frequent Molecular Alterations
- Telomerase maintenance
- TERT promoter mutations
- CTNNB1/Wnt-Beta-catenin pathway activation
- p53 mutations
- MAP kinase signaling

## Targetable Pathways
- c-MET activation
- Fibroblast growth factor receptor
- Vascular endothelial growth factor receptor
- Transforming growth factor beta
- Explored in translational research
- Targeted therapies discussed in treatment section

## Proliferative vs Nonproliferative Classes
- First molecular-based classification divided HCC into two classes
- Proliferative class:
  - Activation of RAS pathway
  - FGF amplification
  - HBV infection
  - Poor prognosis
- Nonproliferative class:
  - Wnt-Beta-catenin alterations
  - HCV infection

## Whole-Genome Integrated Clusters
- Three HCC integrated clusters identified
- Cluster 1:
  - Low mutation frequency of CTNNB1
  - Low expression of TERT
  - Associated with early stage and Asian origin
- Clusters 2 and 3:
  - Higher prevalence of TERT promoter and CTNNB1 mutations
- Cluster 3 also presents with high p53 mutations

## Driver vs Passenger Events
- Limitation of molecular profiling
- Need to distinguish driver events from passenger events
- Driver events are fundamental for neoplastic transformation
- Driver events have potential therapeutic applicability
- Passenger events are not fundamental
- This distinction is challenging

## Heterogeneity and Clinical Translation
- Genetic variations are heterogeneous through time
- Heterogeneous between tumor sites in same individual
- Heterogeneous within a single tumor site
- Advances in molecular characterization have not yet translated into substantial clinical changes
- Precision oncology not yet standard in HCC

## Screening Strategies: Purpose
- Reduce mortality through early detection
- Detect at a stage amenable to curative treatment
- Several uncontrolled studies suggest benefit
- Higher proportion of early diagnoses
- Higher cure rates
- Better prognosis

## Evidence for Screening
- Chinese study of more than 18,000 participants
- Randomized patients with chronic HBV infection
- Screening with ultrasound and serum AFP every 6 months
- HCC mortality significantly reduced in screening group
- 83.2 vs. 131.5 per 100,000 person
- Low adherence among participants
- Carried out in population with HBV

## Selection for Screening
- Determined by risk of developing HCC
- Life expectancy
- Local health structure conditions
- Ability to provide proper treatment
- Cost-effectiveness studies suggest screening when risk is at least 1.5% per year
- Regardless of etiology of liver disease

## Who Should Be Screened
- All patients with cirrhosis who are potential candidates for anti-tumor treatment
- Some subgroups without cirrhosis with chronic HBV infection and high risk
- High-risk scores such as PAGE-B or Toronto-THRI
- Cirrhotic patients with sustained virologic response after HCV treatment
- Must remain under screening because risk is not eliminated

## Who Should Not Be Screened or Uncertain
- Noncirrhotic patients with HCV and bridging fibrosis: unclear
- MAFLD: which subgroups benefit is not defined
- Heterogeneous incidence of HCC within these scenarios
- HCC can arise even in absence of cirrhosis
- More data needed

## Ultrasonography as Screening
- Ultrasonography is screening study of choice
- Balances cost and availability
- Sensitivity 60% to 80%
- Specificity greater than 90%
- Reported for screening liver tumors

## AFP and Other Biomarkers
- Serum AFP measurement commonly applied
- Low sensitivity
- Generally not increased in small tumors
- May be altered by underlying liver disease
- May be altered in cholangiocarcinoma
- Cirrhosis is also risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma
- Primary hepatic mass with increased AFP may be HCC or cholangiocarcinoma
- Other biomarkers: des-y-carboxyprothrombin, AFP-lectin, glypican-3

## Screening Interval
- Recommended interval is semiannual
- Based on estimates of tumor growth rate
- Prospective study showed better performance of 6-month than 12-month interval
- 3-month interval increased detection of small nodules
- No impact on survival
- Role of CT and MRI as screening not yet established

## EASL and AASLD Recommendations
- Abdominal ultrasonography every 6 months
- AFP serum level determination is optional
- Because of suboptimal accuracy of AFP
- Screening widely established in clinical practice for cirrhosis
- Guidelines from European Association for the Study of the Liver
- American Association for Study of Liver Disease

## Clinical Presentation: Spectrum
- Range from asymptomatic to severe symptoms
- Asymptomatic cases often diagnosed in screening programs
- Symptoms may occur because of underlying cirrhosis
- Symptoms may occur because of tumor growth and spread
- Sudden worsening of liver function should be investigated

## Symptoms from Cirrhosis
- Ascites
- Jaundice
- Abdominal collateral circulation
- Upper digestive hemorrhage
- Hepatic encephalopathy

## Symptoms from Tumor Growth
- Abdominal pain
- Weight loss
- Palpable abdominal mass
- Dyspnea
- Bone pain

## Sudden Liver Function Worsening
- In patient with otherwise stable chronic liver disease
- Should be investigated for possibility of HCC
- Ascites and variceal bleeding may develop
- Because of portal or hepatic vein invasion
- Requires prompt evaluation

## Paraneoplastic Syndromes
- Diarrhea
- Hypoglycemia
- Erythrocytosis
- Hypercalcemia
- Generally associated with poor prognosis
- May be present at diagnosis

## Diagnosis: Imaging in Cirrhosis
- Diagnosis can be made using dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging
- Based on neovascularization process during hepatocarcinogenesis
- Malignant lesions develop blood supply from hepatic artery
- Nontumor liver parenchyma supplied predominantly from portal system
- HCC nodules show contrast uptake in arterial phase
- Wash-out in venous and late phases

## Arterial Phase Hyperenhancement and Washout
- Pattern has sensitivity around 80%
- Specificity at least 90%
- In liver nodules larger than 2 cm in context of cirrhosis
- Characteristic vascular profile
- Single dynamic imaging technique can establish diagnosis
- CT or MRI

## Nodules Less Than 1 cm
- May not correspond to malignant focus in greater than 60% of cases
- Close follow-up in 3 to 4 months is recommended
- In cirrhotic liver
- Repeat imaging to assess growth
- Biopsy not usually recommended initially

## Nodules Greater Than 1 cm
- Can be diagnosed as HCC if vascular profile on imaging is typical
- In cirrhotic liver
- Single dynamic imaging technique can establish diagnosis
- If characteristic dynamic profile not recognized
- Fine-needle biopsy is recommended

## Biopsy and Markers
- Biopsy is not 100% sensitive
- Negative result does not exclude HCC
- Other tumor markers proposed:
  - Protein induced by vitamin K absence
  - AFP fractions
  - Glypican-3
- Usefulness in routine clinical practice not established
- Immunohistochemical markers: Hsp-70, glypican-3, glutamine synthetase
- Can increase specificity of histologic diagnosis
- Do not replace expert pathology analysis

## Non-Cirrhotic Liver Diagnosis
- Diagnosis must be made by histology
- Imaging criteria less reliable
- Biopsy needed
- Histologic confirmation important
- Consider other primary liver tumors

## LI-RADS
- Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System
- Proposed by American College of Radiology
- Estimates likelihood of malignancy
- Classifies lesions into 5 categories
- From definitely benign (1) to definitely malignant (5)
- Objective: provide guidance for subsequent management
- Useful for homogeneous reporting
- Prospective studies awaited

## Staging and Prognostic Evaluation: Overview
- Majority of HCC patients have associated liver disease
- Prognostic evaluation should assess tumor extent
- Also assess severity of liver function impairment
- Performance status is key determinant of survival
- Cancer-related symptoms are key determinants
- Several systems and algorithms proposed

- CLPI: Chinese University Prognostic Index
- JIS: Japan Integrated Scoring
- LCSGJ: Liver Cancer Study Group of Japan
- PIVKA: protein induced by vitamin K absence or antagonist
- PS: performance status
- SLiDe: S, stage; L, liver damage; De, des-gamma carboxy prothrombin score
- TNM: tumor-node-metastasis classification
- IUCC: Union Internationale Contre Cancer

## BCLC Strategy
- Widely validated in assessing prognosis
- Incorporates tumor burden, liver function, and cancer-related symptoms
- Original version in 1999
- Updated over years
- Includes five stages: 0, A, B, C, D
- Links staging, prognosis prediction, clinical decision-making, and treatment indication
- Widely accepted clinical tool
- Outperforms other prognosis systems

## BCLC 0 and A
- Very early (BCLC 0): single tumor up to 2 cm
- Early (BCLC A): single lesion irrespective of size or up to 3 nodules up to 3 cm
- Absence of vascular invasion
- Absence of cancer symptoms
- Preserved liver function
- Consider local treatments with curative intention
- Surgical resection, liver transplantation, or percutaneous ablation
- 5-year survival ranges from 50% to 70%

## BCLC B
- Intermediate stage
- Multifocal tumors
- Preserved liver function
- Consider transarterial chemoembolization
- May achieve 50% survival rate at 3 years
- Tumors should be selectively approached
- Prevent damage to non-tumoral liver
- Liver disease should be compensated
- No clinically relevant ascites in need of treatment
- Diffuse, infiltrative, or extensive bilobar involvement: consider systemic therapies

## BCLC C
- Advanced stage
- Preserved liver function
- One or more of:
  - Extrahepatic dissemination
  - Vascular invasion
  - Nonsevere impairment of functionality (ECOG 1-2)
- Benefit from systemic treatment
- Aim to increase survival and improve quality of life
- Sequences of systemic agents provide extended overall survival around 2 years

## BCLC D
- Terminal stage
- Liver dysfunction or severe functional impairment
- ECOG 3-4
- Dismal prognosis
- Should receive best supportive care
- Minimize symptoms
- Focus on quality of life

## Treatment Approaches: Multidisciplinary
- Appropriate treatment selection is complex
- Patients should ideally be managed in reference centers
- Multidisciplinary teams including:
  - Hepatologists
  - Surgeons
  - Radiologists
  - Pathologists
  - Radiation oncologists
  - Clinical oncologists
- Level of evidence limited for many modalities
- Randomized studies in intermediate and advanced stages
- Major research needed

## Treatment Modalities Overview
- Local: resection, transplantation, ablation
- Intra-arterial: TACE, TARE
- Systemic: tyrosine kinase inhibitors, monoclonal antibodies, immunotherapy
- Guidelines and algorithms useful for conceptualization and standardization
- Approach should be personalized
- According to each individual context

## Surgery: Indications
- Liver resection is treatment of choice for localized HCC in absence of cirrhosis
- Patients with compensated cirrhosis should be thoroughly evaluated
- Risk of decompensation
- Severe liver dysfunction: surgery formally contraindicated
- Assessment of liver function is crucial
- Postoperative mortality significantly reduced with normal bilirubin and absence of clinically significant portal hypertension

## Surgery: Liver Function Assessment
- Thromboembryopenia
- Esophageal varices
- Ascites
- Splenomegaly
- Indirect markers of portal hypertension
- Hepatic vein catheterization is most accurate tool
- Hepatic pressure gradient less than 10 mm Hg is best cutoff
- Clinically significant portal hypertension may be established by elastography
- Avoids need for hepatic vein catheterization

## Surgery: Portal Hypertension
- Patients with portal hypertension are at high risk for liver decompensation and death after surgery
- 5-year survival rates of 50%
- Selected patients without portal hypertension: 5-year survival 70% to 80%
- Careful selection essential
- Multidisciplinary evaluation

## Surgery: Tumor Factors
- Optimal results with resection in single lesions
- Selected cases with two or three nodules may be considered
- After careful evaluation
- Tumor size is not a limiting factor
- Risk of recurrence is higher the larger the tumor
- Vascular invasion denotes elevated risk of systemic recurrence
- Should ideally be managed with systemic therapy
- Some groups advocate resection for segmental vascular invasion

## Surgery: Intraoperative Ultrasound and Laparoscopy
- Underestimation of tumour extension is possible
- Intraoperative ultrasound essential
- Detects potential unrecognised nodules between 0.5 and 1 cm
- Optimizes surgical resection efficacy
- Instrumental to perform anatomical resections
- Advances in laparoscopic-robotic surgery allow less invasive treatment
- Comparable survival with lower perioperative morbidity and shorter hospital stays

## Surgery: Recurrence and Adjuvant Therapy
- Disease recurrence after resection may be predicted by pathologic findings
- Poor differentiation degree
- Presence of satellites/multifocality
- Microvascular invasion
- High risk of recurrence
- BCLC proposed enlistment for transplantation in resected HCC with pejorative histologic markers
- No proof of benefit of any adjuvant therapy to prevent recurrence
- No approach should be recommended

## Liver Transplantation: Rationale
- Approaches both tumor and underlying liver disease
- Recommended as first-line option for HCC within Milan criteria
- Best outcomes in carefully selected patients
- Curative intent
- Requires lifelong immunosuppression
- Organ availability limits widespread use

## Milan Criteria
- 1 nodule less than or equal to 5 cm
- Or up to 3 nodules less than or equal to 3 cm
- Absence of portal invasion
- Absence of extrahepatic disease
- Widely used
- Within Milan criteria: 5-year survival 60% to 80%
- Recurrence rate less than 15%
- AFP greater than 1000 ng/mL associated with high risk of recurrence

## Expanded Criteria and AFP
- Increasing data suggest potential benefit of liver transplantation in larger tumor burden
- University of California San Francisco expanded criteria
- AFP level can be used
- Levels greater than 1000 ng/mL associated with high risk of recurrence
- Careful selection remains essential
- Downstaging can increase eligibility

## Bridging and Downstaging
- Bridging therapies: TACE or ablation
- Often needed for patients on waiting list
- Reduce risk of tumor progression
- Especially when time on list longer than 6 months
- Downstaging using locoregional therapies
- Can increase eligibility for liver transplantation
- Key issue: criteria for staging and potential downstaging
- Results variable due to differences in eligibility criteria
- Successful downstaging can reach up to 90% with strict criteria

## Living Donor Liver Transplantation
- Offers possibility to avoid waiting lists for deceased organ
- Important benefit in HCC patients
- Reduces dropout rate and time to transplant
- Potential access for patients not eligible for deceased-donor liver according to Milan criteria
- Must be restricted to centers of excellence
- Minimize donor risk
- Optimize recipient outcome

## Percutaneous Ablation
- Proposed for patients with liver-only disease
- Not candidates for surgery or transplantation
- Radiofrequency and microwave ablation are main techniques
- Ethanol injection can be used in particular situations
- Subcapsular location
- Vicinity of gallbladder, blood vessels, or heart
- Best results in solitary tumors smaller than 2 cm
- May achieve complete necrosis and recurrence rates comparable to resection
- Tumors 2 to 3 cm or up to three nodules may also be treated percutaneously
- Resection not superior to ablation in tumors up to 3 cm in some studies
- Further comparative trials needed

## External Radiotherapy and SBRT
- External radiotherapy and stereotactic body radiation therapy explored
- Some settings: segmental portal vein invasion
- Encouraging results
- Still lacks robust evidence on safety and efficacy

## Intra-arterial Therapy: Rationale
- Patients with liver-only HCC without vascular invasion
- Not amenable to resection, transplantation, or ablation
- Should be considered for intra-arterial therapies
- Aim to induce tumor necrosis
- Exploit predominant arterial blood supply of HCC
- Allows selective infusion of embolizing particles
- Coupled or not with cytotoxic agents
- Or intraarterial infusion of radioactive isotopes

## TACE
- Transarterial chemoembolization
- Intra-arterial drug-eluting beads slowly release chemotherapy
- Conventional chemoembolization uses emulsion of cytotoxic agents with lipiodol followed by spongostan injection
- Similar efficacy
- Drug-eluting beads suggested to have less toxicity and better tolerance
- Both techniques preferred over bland embolization
- No firm evidence to support superiority of one over another
- Randomized trials and metanalysis confirmed TACE improves survival in cases not suitable for curative treatment
- Expected median survival around 30 months
- May exceed 40 months

## TACE Contraindications and Follow-up
- Absolute contraindications:
  - Decompensated cirrhosis
  - Severely reduced portal vein flow
  - Tumoral or nontumoral portal vein thrombosis
- Crucial to assess liver function before and after every procedure
- Prevent liver function deterioration
- In absence of objective response to TACE or untreatable progression
- Systemic therapy should be considered as part of stage migration strategy

## TARE
- Transarterial radioembolization
- Uses injection of 90-Yttrium-labeled spheres
- Without need for macroembolization
- No robust randomized studies comparing TARE with TACE
- Data suggest comparable tumor control rates
- In BCLC C stage, TARE was not superior to sorafenib
- Failed to enhance benefit of sorafenib in combination
- More studies needed to place TARE into treatment algorithms
- Define subgroups that benefit

## Systemic Treatment: Indications
- Recommended for patients with preserved liver function
- Extrahepatic spread
- Macrovascular invasion
- Ineligible for liver-directed modalities because of refractoriness or contraindication

## Early Systemic Therapy History
- Until 2007, limited therapies for advanced stage disease
- Conventional chemotherapy: doxorubicin and platinum combinations
- Significant toxicities and modest efficacy
- Resurgence of enthusiasm with increasing knowledge
- Molecular mechanisms
- Intracellular signaling pathways
- Angiogenesis
- Molecularly targeted agents: sorafenib and regorafenib
- Proved survival superiority over supportive care
- Pioneered era of systemic treatment in HCC

## Sorafenib and Regorafenib
- Sorafenib: tyrosine kinase inhibitor with antiangiogenic and antiproliferative activity
- First drug to demonstrate increased overall survival in advanced HCC
- Survival benefit shown in Western and Asian populations
- Regorafenib: significant increase in survival in advanced HCC progressing on sorafenib
- Sequence sorafenib-regorafenib provided median survival of 26 months
- Reflects significant advance in treatment of advanced HCC

## Lenvatinib and Later-Line Agents
- Lenvatinib: tyrosine kinase inhibitor
- Noninferior to sorafenib in first line
- Approved as alternative to sorafenib
- After progression to sorafenib:
  - Regorafenib
  - Cabozantinib
  - Both as second- or third-line
- Ramucirumab in patients with AFP of at least 400 ng/mL
- Based on positive results of phase III trials

## Immunotherapy
- Liver is complex immunologic organ
- Physiologic immunotolerance
- Abundance of immunosuppressive molecules such as PD-1 and PD-L1
- HCC develops mostly under chronic inflammation
- Immunity-modulating therapies studied in many active clinical trials
- Preliminary results with anti-PD1 antibodies: nivolumab and pembrolizumab
- Encouraging response rates
- Did not compare favorably with sorafenib in first line
- Did not compare favorably with placebo in second line

## Combination Therapies
- Combinations of targeted therapies and immunotherapy gaining prominence
- Atezolizumab (anti-PDL1) plus bevacizumab (anti-VEGF)
- Improved survival in phase 3 trial in first-line versus sorafenib
- Included HCC patients with very well preserved liver function
- Durvalumab (anti-PDL1) plus single dose of tremelimumab (anti-CTLA-4)
- Improved survival over sorafenib
- Durvalumab noninferior to sorafenib
- Other combinations: nivolumab plus ipilimumab; lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab

## Standard of Care and Adverse Events
- Standard of care in advanced HCC based on:
  - Selection of candidates
  - Performance status
  - Liver function
  - Degree of portal hypertension
  - Comorbidities
- Definition of most suitable sequence of drugs
- Expected incidence and severity of adverse events
- Some adverse events such as dermatology reaction under sorafenib or regorafenib
- Associated with better outcomes
- Should be seen positively and not as unnecessary treatment interruptions

## Future Prospects: Prevention
- Prevention of HCC in patients with chronic liver disease is essential
- Advances achieved with antiviral treatment and HBV vaccination
- Trend toward increasing rates of MAFLD-related HCC
- Need to broaden preventive focus
- Causes of metabolic syndrome: obesity, diabetes, dyslipidemia

## Future Prospects: Biomarkers and Early Detection
- Novel biomarkers and imaging tools may allow detection
- Dysplastic nodules before malignant transformation
- Early-stage disease suitable for curative treatment
- Early diagnosis implies better outcomes
- Even after local treatment, recurrence is a concern
- Close follow-up warranted
- Some local recurrences still suitable for curative treatment

## Future Prospects: Adjuvant and Recurrence
- Adjuvant treatments such as immune-oncology agents
- Promising strategies to be tested
- Many recurrences occur outside the liver
- Significant proportion of patients still diagnosed at advanced stage
- Need for effective adjuvant therapies
- Prevention of recurrence is major research area

## Future Prospects: Systemic and Personalized Medicine
- Systemic treatment is probably the most evolving field in HCC
- Moving from no effective drugs in early 2000s
- To several options today
- Active translational research should help develop predictive biomarkers
- Opens doors to personalized medicine and precision oncology
- Already in place in many neoplasms
- Not yet in primary liver cancer

## Figure 89.4: Preventive Measures
- Primary:
  - HBV vaccination
  - Educational programs
  - Anti-alcohol campaigns
  - Control of diabetes, obesity, and dyslipidemia
  - Testing high-risk groups for viral hepatitis
  - Reduce aflatoxin exposure
- Secondary:
  - Semiannual screening
  - Anti-viral therapy
  - Stop alcohol
- Tertiary:
  - Post-treatment monitoring
  - Screening for recurrence
  - Management of adverse events

## Figure 89.4: Active Treatment
- Healthy liver: Diabetes therapy, dyslipidemia therapy, treatment of alcohol use disorders, treatment for obesity
- Chronic disease: Liver transplantation, antiviral therapy, control of metabolic risk factors, treatment of alcohol use disorders
- Cirrhosis: Local therapies, intra-arterial treatment, liver transplantation, systemic treatment
- Liver-only HCC: Local therapies, intra-arterial treatment, liver transplantation, systemic treatment
- Advanced-stage HCC: Systemic treatment

## Figure 89.4: Supportive Measures
- Primary: Primary care follow-up, specialists support when required, governmental engagement, medical societies activity
- Secondary: Specialist follow-up, screening for other cirrhosis complications, variceal bleeding, ascites, etc.
- Tertiary: Multidisciplinary follow-up, cancer symptoms control, management of cirrhosis complications, palliative care

## Figure 89.4: Areas of Research
- Primary: Prophylaxis (statins, aspirin, coffee, etc.), mass screening for viral hepatitis
- Secondary: Identify at-risk groups for screening, methods for screening, molecular risk scores, chemoprophylaxis
- Tertiary: Personalized therapies, predictive biomarkers, prevention of recurrence

## Key Takeaways: Epidemiology
- HCC is a major global health problem
- Incidence varies geographically
- Cirrhosis is the major determinant
- HBV, HCV, alcohol, and MAFLD are main etiologies
- Risk factors are changing with vaccination, DAAs, and metabolic syndrome
- 5-year survival remains low at 5% to 15%

## Key Takeaways: Diagnosis and Screening
- Screening with ultrasound every 6 months is recommended for at-risk patients
- AFP is optional due to low sensitivity
- Diagnosis in cirrhosis relies on dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging
- Arterial hyperenhancement and washout are characteristic
- Biopsy for equivocal cases
- LI-RADS provides standardized reporting

## Key Takeaways: Staging
- BCLC staging is widely validated
- Incorporates tumor burden, liver function, and performance status
- Stages 0, A, B, C, D
- Links staging to treatment recommendation
- Outperforms other prognostic systems
- Table 89.1 summarizes many prognostic systems

## Key Takeaways: Treatment
- Curative options: resection, transplantation, ablation
- Intermediate stage: TACE
- Advanced stage: systemic therapy
- Multiple systemic agents available
- Combinations of targeted therapy and immunotherapy are promising
- Multidisciplinary management is essential
- Personalized approach according to individual context

## Summary
- Hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common primary liver tumor
- Global burden remains high
- Prevention and screening are critical
- Diagnosis relies on imaging in cirrhosis
- BCLC staging guides prognosis and treatment
- Treatment options are expanding
- Future directions include biomarkers, immunotherapy, and personalized medicine
- Multidisciplinary care is key to improving outcomes
